articles.author: Teona
articles.description:
Deciding on the right type of security for your business goes beyond just hiring personnel. Armed security guards are trained to respond to high-risk situations and provide a strong deterrent against serious threats, making them suitable for banks, government buildings, or facilities with valuable assets. On the other hand, unarmed security guards offer a visible presence, manage conflicts, and are often ideal for retail stores, offices, and other low- to medium-risk environments — all at a lower cost and with reduced liability.
Modern security strategies increasingly combine personnel with technology. Tools like Vigilfy allow businesses to schedule shifts, track incidents, and monitor guard performance in real time, helping to ensure that both safety and efficiency are maintained.
When making decisions about security, it’s important to assess your risks, prioritize high-risk areas, and consider hybrid solutions that balance armed and unarmed personnel with surveillance and access control systems. This approach helps protect employees, customers, and assets, while keeping costs manageable and ensuring legal compliance.
By taking a thoughtful, strategic approach to security, business owners can make informed choices that meet their needs today while preparing for potential risks tomorrow.


  
  
  ArmedSecurityGuards #UnarmedSecurityGuards #ModernSecurity #BusinessSafety #RiskManagement #Vigilfy #SecurityPlanning #EmployeeSafety #AssetProtection
articles.title: Choosing Between Armed and Unarmed Security Guards: What Business Owners Should Know

articles.author: Edvaldo Freitas
articles.description:
Technical debt isn’t a monster that suddenly appears after a "bad sprint." It's a cumulative tax you pay on every future feature. It's born in the small, seemingly harmless decisions we make every day. The shortcut taken, the confusing variable name, the test case we skipped "just this once." The most effective strategy for reducing technical debt isn't a massive refactoring project; it's changing how you handle every single pull request.
Most teams treat the PR as the last checkpoint before merging. CI is green? Ship it. But this misses the point. The PR is the single best leverage point you have to prevent debt from ever taking root. It's where code, context, and team standards collide. It’s a moment for collaboration and quality control, not just a rubber stamp.
